passage:
At the wedding hall in Leicester, Mateo's Nani steered him from chair to chair. 'Touch Masi's feet. Now Mamaji's. Now this uncle's.' Mateo, nine, had never seen half of them. His knees hurt, his cheeks burned, and one uncle's shoes smelled of polish. He glanced at his cousin Rania, who was hiding behind a pillar to escape the same thing. When Nani pointed him toward yet another stranger, Mateo whispered, 'Why do I have to?'
Mum crouched beside him. 'It's a way of saying you respect them, but it only means something if you want to. You can do namaste instead.'
Mateo folded his hands to the stranger, who smiled and blessed him anyway.

qa.q: Where was the wedding?
qa.a: At the wedding hall in Leicester.

qa.q: How was Mateo feeling as Nani steered him from chair to chair?
qa.a: He felt embarrassed and uneasy, bowing to people he barely knew, with sore knees and burning cheeks.

qa.q: What did Mum do that helped, and why?
qa.a: She explained that touching feet is respect that should be willing, and offered namaste instead, easing his discomfort without dropping respect.

qa.q: How might Nani see Mateo's question 'Why do I have to?'
qa.a: Nani may feel a little hurt or worried that the custom is slipping, since introducing him to every relative feels like love and duty to her.

grounding: Shows a child told to touch the feet of relatives he barely knows at a wedding, who feels embarrassed until a parent explains the gesture is voluntary respect.

passage:
On Monday, during circle time in Class 4, Usha said her weekend was 'the worst'. 'At my cousin's wedding, Amma made me touch the feet of forty people. Some I didn't even know. One aunty laughed because I did it wrong.' Her voice wobbled.
Harsha Ma'am didn't laugh. 'That sounds embarrassing. Did you want to do it?'
'For Paati, yes. Not for strangers.'
Ma'am nodded. 'Touching feet is meant to show respect you really feel. You can also greet with folded hands and a smile. Maybe tell Amma how it felt?'
Usha thought for a moment. 'Tomorrow. When she's not busy.'

qa.q: How many people did Usha have to bow to?
qa.a: Forty people.

qa.q: How did Usha feel describing the wedding, and what shows it?
qa.a: Usha felt embarrassed and uneasy; her voice wobbled, especially remembering the aunty who laughed.

qa.q: What did Harsha Ma'am do well?
qa.a: She listened without laughing, named the feeling, explained that bowing should be respect you really feel, and suggested talking to Amma.

qa.q: How might Amma react when Usha explains how it felt?
qa.a: Amma might be surprised, but could see that Usha truly respects Paati and let Usha greet strangers with folded hands instead.

grounding: Illustrates a child made to touch the feet of many barely known relatives at a wedding who feels embarrassed, and a teacher who explains the gesture as voluntary respect.

passage:
Friday: "At the wedding, you touch every elder's feet. Everyone," Mummy said. Himani, ten, counted on her fingers and ran out of fingers.

Saturday: Forty relatives, half of them strangers. Himani bent and bent until her face was hot. One uncle didn't even look down. When Irfan Uncle, Papa's old friend, saw her bending again, he smiled. "Namaste is plenty, beta."

Sunday: On the drive home, Mummy asked why she was so quiet. Himani told her. Mummy was silent a moment, then said, "It's meant to be respect you choose, not a queue. Next time, bow to the ones you mean it for, and namaste the rest."

At home Himani touched Nani's feet on her own, slowly.

qa.q: How many relatives were at the wedding?
qa.a: Forty relatives, half of them strangers.

qa.q: What was Himani feeling as she kept bending at the wedding?
qa.a: Himani felt embarrassed and uneasy, her face hot, bowing to strangers who didn't even look down.

qa.q: What did Mummy's explanation give Himani?
qa.a: It told her the gesture is respect she chooses, so she can bow to those she means it for and greet others with a namaste.

qa.q: How might Irfan Uncle have seen Himani's bending?
qa.a: Irfan Uncle noticed she looked uncomfortable and kindly let her off with a namaste.

grounding: Shows a child told to touch the feet of every relative at a wedding, feeling embarrassed, and helped by learning the gesture is chosen respect.

passage:
Devika, stop scowling at the wedding card and listen to your Bhavna Nani.

When I was nine, at my cousin's wedding in Udaipur, my mother marched me from elder to elder. "Pair chhoo, pair chhoo." Sixty people. My back ached, my face burned, and one old man smelled of snuff.

Halfway through I started crying behind the tent. My grandmother found me there. I thought she would scold me. Instead she wiped my face and said, "Touching feet is a gift you give. A gift given by force is no gift. Choose whose feet you want to touch. Fold your hands to the others. That is respect too."

I went back and chose four people. I remember each of them still.

So at Gauri's wedding, you choose too.

qa.q: How many people did Bhavna's mother march her to?
qa.a: Sixty people.

qa.q: What was young Bhavna feeling behind the tent?
qa.a: She felt embarrassed and overwhelmed, her back aching and face burning, and afraid she would be scolded.

qa.q: What turning point changed that wedding for young Bhavna?
qa.a: Her grandmother, instead of scolding, explained that touching feet is a gift you choose, so she went back and chose four people.

qa.q: How might Bhavna's grandmother have seen the crying girl?
qa.a: She saw a child pushed into an empty routine, and cared more about the girl's feelings than the count.

grounding: Shows a child made to touch dozens of relatives' feet at a wedding, and an elder explaining that the gesture is voluntary respect.

passage:
The baraat was twenty minutes late, the photographer was shouting, and Masi kept pushing Parul, eight, toward a row of strangers from the groom's side. "Quick, quick, touch feet, all of them!"

Parul bent to the first, then the second. Her new lehenga caught under her sandal and she nearly fell. Someone laughed. Her ears went red, and she stopped, arms stiff, staring at the shoes.

Her cousin Himani, fifteen, crouched beside her. "You don't have to do all of them," she whispered. "Fold your hands and say namaste. It's still respect."

Parul folded her hands. The next old lady smiled and blessed her just the same.

qa.q: How late was the baraat?
qa.a: The baraat was twenty minutes late.

qa.q: Why did Parul stop, arms stiff, staring at the shoes?
qa.a: Parul felt embarrassed and anxious after nearly falling and hearing someone laugh, and uneasy bowing to so many strangers in a rush.

qa.q: How did Himani help, and what could Masi do next time?
qa.a: Himani calmly offered namaste as a respectful choice; Masi could explain the same before the rush instead of pushing.

qa.q: How might the old lady see Parul's namaste?
qa.a: She sees it as real respect, and blesses Parul just the same.

grounding: Shows a child hurried into touching strangers' feet at a wedding, feeling embarrassed, and a cousin explaining that a namaste is respect too.

passage:
The wedding hall in Lucknow was full of shiny saris and loud music. "Ujjwal, touch Mamaji's feet. Now Bade Nanaji. Now that aunty." Mummy kept steering him by the shoulder. Ujjwal, ten, bent again and again. Some of these people he had never seen. By the twentieth person, Ujjwal's cheeks were burning. He hid behind a pillar.
Indu Bua found him there. "Tired of bending?" He nodded, eyes stinging. "I don't even know them." Bua sat on the steps beside him. "Touching feet is a way to show respect you feel. It isn't a punishment. For people you don't know, a namaste is fine." Ujjwal looked up. "Mummy will be angry." "I'll talk to her," Bua said. She did. After that, Ujjwal did namaste for strangers and touched Nanaji's feet properly, slowly, because he loved Nanaji.

qa.q: Where did Ujjwal hide?
qa.a: Behind a pillar.

qa.q: How did Ujjwal feel by the twentieth person?
qa.a: He felt embarrassed and uneasy, his cheeks burning, bowing to people he didn't know.

qa.q: How did Indu Bua help Ujjwal?
qa.a: She explained that touching feet is voluntary respect, offered namaste as a choice for strangers, and spoke to Mummy for him.

qa.q: How might Mummy have seen her steering at the wedding?
qa.a: Mummy probably wanted Ujjwal to show good manners in front of the family and didn't notice how uneasy it made him.

grounding: It illustrates a child told to touch every relative's feet at a wedding who feels uneasy, and an adult who explains the gesture is voluntary respect.
